# English for presentations

## Match the reading situation

For a live presentation, listeners divide attention between the screen and the
speaker. Show the message and evidence they need now; reserve explanatory detail
for speaker notes. For a read-alone deck, retain enough context on the slide for
someone who cannot hear the talk. A PDF recipient may never see the notes.

Do not silently change agreed slide count, sequence, sources or required images.
If wording alone cannot solve overload, propose a split or appendix and explain
what would move. Editing is not permission to redesign the story or invent evidence.

## Headlines carry the right claim

- Use sentence case unless the house style or an official title requires otherwise.
  For an evidence slide, prefer a specific assertion that the visual supports.
  Covers, agenda pages, labels and section dividers can use short noun phrases.
- Use a question when the answer is genuinely unresolved. Do not turn `may reduce`
  into `reduces`, a planned action into an achieved result, or a topic into a
  confident claim just to make the headline stronger.
- Keep enough English grammar to identify the relationship. Do not remove articles,
  auxiliaries or subjects mechanically to reach a word count. A label such as
  `Approval status` is fine; a claim that needs decoding is not.
- Treat one or two display lines as a fit check, not a fixed character allowance.
  English words differ in width and length. Put the useful point early, but retain
  a condition in the headline or visibly next to it when that condition changes
  the meaning. Never write an unconditional headline contradicted only in notes.
- Read the sequence of headlines. They should form a supported explanation, not
  a series of generic promises or unrelated slogans.

## Body and bullets

Keep one job per item. Use parallel verbs for instructions, parallel noun phrases
for categories, or parallel sentences for findings. Preserve mixed roles when
the source needs them, but label those roles instead of manufacturing symmetry.
Do not pad a list to three items or delete a real fourth item for rhythm.

A shared lead-in must combine grammatically with every bullet. Do not let `must`
in a heading convert advisory items into requirements. Use numbered lists for
an actual order and bullets for peers. Full-sentence bullets generally need
sentence punctuation; short labels need not. Apply the house style consistently.

Use lists for scanning and short prose for an explanation whose logic would be
lost in fragments. There is no universal bullet percentage or six-by-six rule.
Avoid heavy bold labels that merely repeat the following words; retain labels
that help compare options. Do not make the screen a transcript of the talk.

## Evidence, charts and labels

- Check units, denominator, time window, comparison baseline and attribution.
  Define acronyms for the intended audience, not every audience imaginable.
- Keep `significant` distinct from `statistically significant` and preserve
  `not statistically significant`. Do not turn a non-significant result into
  proof of no difference. Keep `average`, `median`, `up to` and `at least` distinct.
- Preserve the distinction between percent and percentage points, actual and
  forecast values, and association and causation. Do not add derived arithmetic
  unless calculation is requested and its inputs are established.
- Replace repeated prose with a label only when the visual still identifies the
  actor, measure and relationship. Keep chart labels consistent with the text.
  A short phrase must not collapse distinct entities into the same label.
- Keep source limitations and synthetic-data labels next to the relevant claim.
  Never hide an interpretation-changing caveat in speaker notes or an unreadable
  footnote. Retain meaningful qualifiers when shortening axis titles or legends.

## Speaker notes

Notes support the speaker with the reason, example, transition and likely
question, not a duplicate of every visible bullet. Use spoken English with
manageable clauses and clear referents. Contractions are acceptable when the
speaker's register supports them; do not add conversational fillers or opinions.

Keep visible claims and spoken explanations consistent. Moving information into
notes does not authorize dropping it, changing disclosure boundaries or deleting
machine-readable authoring records. Track any movement by slide ID.

## English line breaks and fit

Break at meaningful phrase or clause boundaries. Avoid isolating an article from
its noun, a modal from its verb, `not` from its predicate, a number from its unit,
or an acronym from its expansion. Prefer a readable two-line phrase to a dense
single line. Do not split a product name or force a one-word final line if a
small wording or frame adjustment can avoid it without changing meaning.

Use real typography settings, not repeated spaces. Inspect the actual font and
frame; do not shrink text or remove a qualifier just to fit. Propose a layout
change or content split if necessary. A grammar check cannot verify visual fit.

In AISlide, return final wording to the execution workflow, which owns typed
edits, revision/hash guards, tool limits, previews and saving. Changing managed
part text may affect regeneration metadata; do not bypass that contract. Do not
claim a PPTX, PDF or speaker view was checked if only plain text was reviewed.
